[[RunningHead]]

Individual Treatment Needs in the Therapeutic Environment of a Special School

John Woods

John Woods

London
25 Park Avenue South London N8

John Woods  

A school which is specially set up* for emotionally and behaviourally disturbed children needs to combine a treatment perspective with educational aims. The philosophy of the school must include an understanding of emotional disturbance if it is to fulfil its main task, namely to educate a child socially and cognitively, and to prepare him or her for work and adult family life. There are however fundamental differences between the philosophy of education and the theory and practice of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Disparities between the two frameworks produce ambiguities that can result in contradictions in practice. These conflicts can hamper the staff group as a whole and may be played out in rivalries between representative disciplines: a chronic split may occur between psychiatric and teaching staff. As a child psychotherapist and former teacher in a special school, I shall here discuss some of the problems in reconciling the two viewpoints. The intention is to go some way nearer to meeting the clinical and educational challenge presented by the disturbed child.

The children and their families

All schools have numbers of children who make poor use of the educational opportunities; they fail to learn from the curriculum and the social experience seems to be inadequate for their needs. Although the blocks to learning would seem to have originated in the child's environment, the school endeavours with all its specialist resources to overcome the internal blocks to learning specific to the child. Some children receive particular attention because they make it impossible, not only for themselves, but for others to benefit from the education in the school. A succession of interventions will have been made: remedial groups, tutorial groups, support units, child guidance referral. Most often, it is through the child's violent and disruptive behaviour and the intolerance of frustration that the school and other agencies come to the conclusion that the child needs to be in a special school for emotionally and behaviourally disturbed children. The child psychiatric diagnosis of conduct disorder combined with, for example, neurotic disorder, is the one that is most usually employed to describe the manifest problem.

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows  

The main aim of Bettelheim's latest book is to try and help us see the real Freud behind the mis-translations of the Standard Edition. He demonstrates most persuasively how the Stracheys have tried to impose a pseudo-scientific veneer over Freud's deliberately everyday choice of language. All of their mis-renderings tend in this same direction and many examples are given including some of those that have become most deeply embedded in the language of psycho-analysis. The most obvious are the terms “ego”, “id” and “superego” which in the original are “ich”, “es” and “überich”. These have, of course, their everyday English equivalents (“me” or “I”, “it”, “above — I”) and there are no grounds for supposing that there is any reason to translate them otherwise (the French, for example, use “moi”, “ca” and “surmoi” as direct equivalents). Other examples include “cathexis”, and “parapraxis”, even “free association”. But I shall not repeat here all of Bettelheim's cogent instances.

The essence of the distortion is represented in the title of Bettelheim's book: Freud was profoundly concerned with the study of man's soul and the instrument he used, primarily, was his self-analysis.

151

Marie Winn: Children Without Childhood, Growing Up Too Fast in the World of Sex and Drugs. Published by Penguin Books, 1984. Paperback, £2.95.

Frances Salo

Frances Salo

Frances Salo  

Ms Winn's book is a clarion call to American parents. Its thesis, succinctly contained in the title, is as follows: since the 1960s a radical change has occurred in the way American society treats children and in the behaviour of children themselves. Adults have abandoned their traditional role of protectors of childhood innocence and encouraged an early involvement in adult concerns, thus transforming the image of childhood from one that deserves protection to one that justifies their own sometimes monstrous abandonment of children. In the last few decades there are signs among adults of increasing ambivalence, if not hostility, towards children (seen in films depicting child pornography, prostitution and satanic juveniles). Current child-rearing trends which emphasize equality and shared decision-making have helped to produce children who are often more difficult to live with than their more repressed counterparts, and who may engender murderous wishes in parents.

At the heart of parental loss of control lies the fact that parents today supervise their school-age children less than would have been the case a generation ago, as a result of the increase of two-career families and divorce — currently one in two couples in the U.S.A. The combination of unsupervised children and a permissive, highly charged sexual atmosphere, particuarly disseminated by television, and the influx of easily acquired drugs, has led to a generation of what Ms Winn calls children without childhood (innocence), i.e. prematurely sophisticated out-of-control children and adolescents.

In Memoriam Marie Battle Singer

Ann Bolt

Ann Bolt

Ann Bolt  

Marie Singer died in Cambridge, England, in May 1985. She was born in Mississippi. She took her degree at Smith College, Cambridge, Massachusetts and then qualified as a psychiatric social worker. She came to Europe after the War to do social work in Germany and then decided to become a child psychotherapist. She became a student at the Hampstead Child Therapy Clinic in 1950, qualifying in 1954. She was a friend of Karin Stephen and it was in the Bloomsbury group of writers and analysts that she met her husband, the poet and marine biologist James Burns Singer. They moved to Cambridge in 1959 where she made an immediate impact. As the only practising child psychotherapist in Cambridge Marie Singer was greatly in demand, not only as a therapist but also as a teacher. One of her great gifts — and she was also a very gifted therapist — was her ability to bring psychodynamic concepts to interested but uninformed people. She was the first person to lecture to undergraduates in this way in the Psychology course in the Moral Sciences Tripos, and this was in a primarily behaviourally orientated psychology school. She conducted on-going group seminars for doctors in Cambridge which resulted in a number of recruits to psychiatry and psychoanalysis. She was made a Fellow of Clare Hall, a distinction in which she took enormous pride and pleasure.

For many years she was a child psychotherapist in the Department of Child Psychiatry at the Middlesex Hospital. Her willingness to accept the most difficult cases and her ready and generous discussion of therapeutic difficulties of other members of staff was invaluable. She reacted to the sudden and premature death of her husband with courage and resilience, and we are left with memories of a vivacious and charismatic personality who made psychodynamic concepts live for a large number of people. She will be remembered with gratitude and affection.

[[RunningHead]]

A Study of the Component Elements in the Establishment of Limits: Their Evolution in the Treatment of an Anorexic Baby

Cleopatre Athanassiou

Cleopatre Athanassiou

9 rue Delouvain
75019 Paris

Cleopatre Athanassiou  

Bruno was a premature baby, three weeks before term, but his development could be described as satisfactory. His mother was disappointed when she discovered she could not breast-feed this first-born child. Bruno had troubles sleeping during his first month, but these difficulties subsided in the second month. Then something happened at two months. Bruno's mother received a telephone call from the crèche where she had reserved a place for Bruno so she could return to work: there was an opening for Bruno in two weeks. The mother broke down upon hearing this news. The Directress of the crèche informed me later, “When I received her she was in tears. I even accompanied her to the door, because I was afraid she might fall down the stairs.”

A few days later, about ten days before Bruno was, in fact, to be separated from his mother and enter the crèche, Bruno reacted by catching a cold which quickly turned into bronchitis. He rejected practically all forms of nourishment, including the bottle. His mother returned to work. But Bruno's appetite did not increase in the crèche. Visits to the hospital and examinations did not counter-act his steady loss of weight.

Bruno had been in the crèche for a month when the nurses asked me to have a look at him. He was therefore three and a half months old. Since they asked what his behaviour might reflect, I suggested, rather discreetly, that perhaps Bruno was reacting to his separation from his mother. They immediately responded with, “Do you think he can possibly feel anything at that age? Of course not. He doesn't feel a thing.”

Yet, in spite of what they said, what other hypothesis could be evoked in describing the catastrophe this baby had experienced? As the observation of Bruno will later show, a depression was sustained by both mother and baby when the mother collapsed, a collapse which was experienced by the baby as the object's sudden loss of sight. The mother's arms and body were there, and her face as well, but her communicative eyes, the very essence of life, its movement and its richness, had vanished.

Anne-Marie Sandler

Anne-Marie Sandler

Anne-Marie Sandler  

A few years ago our friend and colleague, Agi Bene-Moses, died in Israel after what seemed a cruelly short time of marital fulfilment. Following her death the idea of putting together a book in her memory took shape. The intended title was “The Self in Childhood”, reflecting Agi's particular interest in borderline children and adults. Many of her friends volunteered contributions, and Isabel Menzies Lyth and Sydney Klein were among them. Unfortunately the high cost of printing and other practical difficulties eventually made the publication of the book impossible. The papers intended for the memorial volume are being published in various places, and I am delighted that some have found a place in the Journal of Child Psychotherapy.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy with a Mentally Handicapped Boy

Robin Balbernie

Robin Balbernie

Poole

Robin Balbernie  

Mentally retarded children are sometimes hemmed in by a sense of “no hope”; and sometimes, too, the helplessness felt within their family becomes part of a spiral wherein this lack of hope threads through the child's inner and outer worlds. Perhaps a part of psychotherapeutic work here is to hold onto enough hope for two, and thus offer a form of auspicious retrieval from that time when the mother's joyful, unspoken, expectations are woven around her newborn baby. Psychotherapy is usually engrossing; maybe it also has to have an element of real pleasure, simply be fun at times, for hope to be accepted back again. This was certainly the case with Nigel, a robust eleven year old with a full scale IQ of 67, who was referrred as a result of his uncontrollable aggression and calculated destructiveness both at home and at school.

Nigel had been born with hypothyroidism, which unfortunately had not been diagnosed sufficiently early for remedial treatment to be attempted. When his condition had been spotted he had a brief period in hospital, just before his first birthday. This was his only separation. His parents had always been caring and supportive of him; but perhaps had slightly over-compensated for the guilt felt about his handicap by not placing the same limits around his behaviour as had been applied to his older brother.

When he had been assessed forspecial education, five years before I saw him, it was noted that he had difficulty in relating to other children, to whom he was often violent without any discernable reason. Everyone appeared to have found him both active and superficially friendly, attention- seeking with adults but at the same time strenuously rejecting any overt display of affection.

Now his school, who had referred him as a last resort, saw Nigel as a “very angry little boy” who spent all his playtime doing nothing but getting into fights with other children. He was literally engaged in indiscriminate assaults all the time, regardless of whether or not he came off worse. The headmaster felt Nigel was “out of control when not at school”, and described him as being furiously opposed to lessons when in.

[[RunningHead]]

(II) Sleep Problems in Babies and Young Children

Dilys Daws

Dilys Daws

43 Heath Hurst Road
London N.W.3

Dilys Daws  

In the preceding article, I described my work in the Baby Clinic of a General Practice. Some of my time there is spent in consulting with the G.P.s and Health Visitors who run the baby clinic about the emotional aspect of the problems they are concerned with in the babies they see.

In the actual clinical work I undertake myself I see families where there is a feeling of not being able to manage a particular state of a baby's or small child's development. The most pressing of these are often presented as sleeping problems. I have seen a number of these and found that about half can be noticeably helped in a short time. One or two consultations allow some change in the parents' approach to the baby that breaks the deadlock between them.

My technique is to combine a structured questioning about the details of the baby's time-table — taking the mother through the minutiae of both day and night — with a free-ranging look at the history of the pregnancy and birth, with the mother's relationship with the father and with her own parents. My impression is that if there is a good marriage or stable relationship, this work is effective if carried out either with the mother alone, or with both parents. With an unsatisfactory relationship the mother alone can be helped, but with this particular technique taking on two disharmonious parents is not usually effective in the short-term. It can however be a focus and starting-off point for parents who are looking for marital help. At times, sleeping problems in their baby appear to expose a lack of real commitment to a long-term relationship in two young unmarried parents.

What strikes me in this work is that by offering a free-floating attention, a particular arresting theme often emerges — a connection that has a compulsive attraction. I am never sure that this is what the problem is “really” about, but pin-pointing it seems to be of significance both for the mother and myself at the time. This is possibly more likely to happen if I see the mother alone. An unconscious thread builds up between the mother and myself so that my line of questioning is informed by the clues she has been giving me and cumulative evidence is built up.

The Kleinian Concept of Position and Group Therapeutic Process: An Experience in Group Psychotherapy with Emotionally Disturbed Boys Aged 6 to 9 12 Years

Elisabeth Muir

Elisabeth Muir

New Zealand

Elisabeth Muir  

Introduction

Reviews of the history and literature of group psychotherapy in general (McLennan & Levy, 1969; Lubin, Lubin & Sargent, 1972; Skynner, 1974; and Silver et al, 1981) make it clear that there is a wide range of techniques and that the conceptual bases for such work are sometimes consistent, sometimes diverse and controversial. In 1950 Ackerman discussed the difficulties inherent in formulating a theoretical frame that would allow for an integration of the processes of individual psychoanalytic and group psychology. This issue was to some extent addressed in 1959 when Bion described group processes as incorporating the paranoid schizoid and depressive positions as conceptualized by Klein (1952). He inferred that group interpretations facilitated the shift from the predominance of basic assumption functioning to a predominance of work group functioning. He did not clearly describe a group developmental process, rather he described fluctuating group states, or modes of group functioning.

Subsequently there have been some descriptions of adult group developmental processes, relating them to the concepts of Bion, Freud, Klein and others (Skynner, 1974; La Coursiere, 1980). In a 1974 review of group therapy, Skynner (p. 235) states, “My own belief is that (there is required to be) more recognition of the natural history of growth and developmental processes in groups …”. He also briefly outlined some future trends which I feel are manifested in the processes discussed in this paper. One trend he referred to is the increasing emphasis and interest in the value of the experiential relative to the intellectual; the non-verbal relative to the verbal. This issue, also discussed by Rosenbluth (1968), is highlighted by the group processes described in the present paper. The other relevant trend Skynner discusses (1974) is the increase in interest in the developmental theories within psychoanalytic theory. He suggests that a group might be expected to work through a sequence of stages corresponding to normal child development … (p. 248) and goes on to relate the process in closed groups to the stages or psychosexual phases of development described by Freud, relating that in turn to the work of Bion and others.

Andrew Samuels, Jung and the Post-Jungians, published by Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1985. Hardback, £14.95.

Sandra Walline

Sandra Walline

Sandra Walline  

This is a book of dialogue — dialogue between and amongst Jung, post-Jungians, psychoanalysts and others. Samuels brings this dialogue to life in a comparative study, comprehensively surveying the developments that have taken place since Jung's death in 1961.

114

Each chapter is organised around an important theme in Jung's work. There are chapters on the schools of analytical psychology; the archetype and complex; the ego; the self and individuation; analytical process; gender, sex and marriage; dreams; and archetypal psychology. In order to illustrate some of these theoretical concepts, another chapter presents clinical material from the author's work with a patient.

In the first chapter, Samuels sets the scene and introduces the schools of analytical psychology, briefly describing the three existing clarifications of post-Jungian schools — Adler, Fordham and Goldenberg, and then outlines his own classification into three main schools — Classical, Developmental and Archetypal. He elaborates this classification into six headings — three theoretical areas (the definition of the archetypal, the concept of the self and the development of personality) and three clinical aspects (the analysis of transference — counter-transference, emphasis upon symbolic experience of the self and examination of highly differentiated imagery).

Each school emphasises different aspects of these six headings and orders them in a different priority; however, taken altogether, Samuels sees these as the common core, or the “Post-Jungian vertex”, with which all analytical psychologists are concerned. This classification, together with the accompanying list of writers of theoretical similarity, is useful for orientating the reader throughout the book.

The content of the remaining chapters is far too complex to outline here, but I want to make a general comment on the masterful way in which the author weaves together various theoretical threads, from a critical presentation of Jung's major indeas, to various post-Jungian views and to comparisons between analytical psychology and psychoanalysis. He also brings in relevant points from other disciplines — ethology, biology, physics, literature, etc., and links similar points found in various parts of the book by parenthetical cross-referencing.

[[RunningHead]]

Referral and Assessment for Psychotherapy in a School for Children with Emotional and Behavioural Difficulties

Susan Dyke

Susan Dyke

21 Croftdown Road
London N.W.5

Susan Dyke  

Introduction

This paper is an investigation into referral and assessment for individual psychotherapy in a day special school for children with emotional and behavioural difficulties. It was written principally for the teachers who work in such schools, who have the problem of choosing whom to refer out of all their needy charges, without the benefit of a therapist's training and experience in how to make this choice. It also includes some exploration of the particular difficulties that beset the therapist in such a setting over the issue of assessment. As a result of the audience for whom it was originally prepared, there is no actual clinical material included, and there is a deliberate avoidance of diagnostic jargon beyond the level with which the school staff-group were likely to be familiar. The paper falls into two distinct parts. The first consists of a discussion of the particular nature of the assessment process in a school setting. The second is a survey of all the children referred for therapy in one school during the two and a half years of my employment there, both those who sustained their therapy and those who did not, in an attempt to clarify the most important issues in referring and assessing these children in this setting. This survey is deliberately comprehensive, with no child omitted, so as to represent accurately the range of cases a school therapist is likely to encounter and the referral issues they raise.

Assessment in a school

First, let us look at the ways in which assessment in a school differs from assessment in a clinic or a hospital. It might be thought that one would still be making the same sort of judgements about a child when assessing them wherever one practises, and that the setting is of little importance. In what ways would the process differ just because one is operating in a school? Despite the fact that the aim of the exercise is ultimately the same wherever one is working, in my experience the difference in setting exerts a very considerable influence on the technique of assessment.

Francis Dale

Francis Dale

Francis Dale  

As the title of this book suggests, its main theme and focus concerns the “shared” nature of analytic work between therapist and client: “Neither therapist nor patient alone can know what is best or what is needed. This is jointly discovered as the therapeutic process unfolds” (p. 179). The notion of mutual reciprocity is not a new idea, and Mr. Casement readily acknowledges the influence of people like R.J. Langs (author of The Listening Process), D. Winnicott, W. Bion and many others. What I think is different about the theoretical concepts and ways of working as outlined in this book, relates not to their uniqueness, but to the fact that the author has managed to bring them together so skilfully and sensitively to produce a coherent, systematic way of clinically appraising oneself, one's client and the interplay between the two.

Mr. Casement repeatedly alerts us to the danger of forcing clients into a theoretical or interpretive straitjacket; and of the value of being able to tolerate “not knowing”, or of “knowing” but learning to wait until the client is receptive to, and able to assimilate, what we have to impart to them. He also points out the role the client plays in this “knowing” and the ways in which the therapist can become maximally aware and receptive to the therapeutic “promptings” from the client: “what is not always acknowledged is that patients also read the unconscious of the therapist” (p. 3).

I find the notion that our clients “monitor” our therapeutic input immensely reassuring. It is a foil to the therapist becoming too omnipotent and the therapy becoming too one way and one-sided. It also means that there are always — or should be — three “people” in the consulting room: the client, the therapist and the “co-therapist” — namely that aspect of the client which is actively engaged in the therapeutic process alongside the therapist. As the author points out:

It is no longer adequate to think of the analyst as the one who observes and interprets, and the patient as the only person in this relationship who presents evidence of unconscious communications and pathology. Patients do not see the analyst as a blank screen. They scrutinise the analyst, who aims to remain inscrutable, and they find many clues to the nature of this person they are dealing with. They sense the state of mind of the analyst and respond accordingly. (p. 57)

Jonathan Bradley

Jonathan Bradley

83 Platts Lane London N.W.3.

Jonathan Bradley  

Background & Initial Meeting with Parents

Omiros was referred to a Child Guidance Unit when he was 4 years 8 months old. At the time of referral he seemed to be living in a fantasy world and his parents felt that they had little contact with him; nor did they have effective control. As the time for him to attend school approached, they had become deeply concerned about other aspects of his behaviour as well. For some time Omiros had been pushing pieces of plastic and wooden bricks into his bottom and he would attempt to do the same to his brother (aged 6 months at referral) or even to the children of social acquaintances if left alone with them. As a result of punishment he had become more secretive about his behaviour and had resorted to smuggling objects in with him when he went to the toilet and to emerging with them inserted in his bottom. By the time he came to the clinic, he had become more secretive, no doubt due to the fact that his parents would search his person from time to time and beat him if guilty.

At a meeting to investigate the possibility of therapy, I was forcibly struck by how helpless his parents felt in the face of such behaviour. They gave a tragic picture of the events leading up to the referral. It must be said, however, that from the beginning some aspects of the case history seemed puzzling and even now the picture is not altogether clear. Omiros's mother, Mrs. C, said that 18 months previously (when O was 2 12) she had been bathing him when she had discovered semen in his anus. She said (with Mr. C present) that a Playgroup worker from the Nursery was suspected of assault and dismissed from his job. Apparently several children were said to be involved. However, a police doctor examined Omiros but said that there was not sufficient evidence for prosecution. Another source of information — the Health Visitor — said that father's lack of concern at the time seemed very suspicious and she thought he might have been involved in some way. It must be said that there has been no direct evidence to support her suspicions. It is still a cloudy area therefore.

Catherine Garvey: Children's Talk. Published by Fontana, 1984. Paperback, £2.95.

Judy Shuttleworth

Judy Shuttleworth

Judy Shuttleworth  

This book is part of The Developing Child series edited by Jerome Bruner, Michael Cole and Barbara Lloyd. The series is a useful source of information about current academic work in child development, a field which is producing work of far greater interest and relevance to psycho-analysis than was once the case. This volume, although giving a glimpse of the Wider field of language research, is chiefly concerned with Catherine Garvey's own study of children's talk. The book is especially readable as the author gives a considerable number of verbatim reports of the conversation of small children, who thus have a chance to come alive for the reader as they struggle to share toys, organize their games and discuss the ways of the world. The research study is presented as throwing light on such conversations rather than taking precedence over them.

Catherine Garvey's study falls into two parts — a larger-scale study of 3-5 year olds observed in a laboratory playroom, and a longitudinal study of three children, aged 2-3 years at the start. These children were videoed both at home and at the laboratory with their “best friend” and their mothers. At least in the form in which it is presented in this book, the size of the study seems to allow for a more individual case study approach rather than a statistical one and the need for standardization and rigour in the research design do not obtrude at the expense of complexity and interest. On the contrary, the author seems to have in mind the study of talk in the hurly-burly of everyday life.

Catherine Garvey refers several times to the work of Erving Goffman, who was a key figure in moving Sociology in the direction of more subtle participant observation methods of research and away from the crudeness of the standardized interview and the large-scale survey. It is this spirit which seems apparent in the following comment about the status of video and audio recordings:

“Talk is a very complex activity. Like other human activities, it unfolds in time. It happens and disappears very rapidly, leaving only a suggestive trace in memory. When we capture it by recordings, in writing or more completely in audio or video recordings, we have a more faithful reproduction of it, although the rehearing is a very different experience from either hearing it or taking part in it as it took place. The analyst can examine a record of talk at leisure and can study the outcome to help interpret what preceded. Participants and over-hearers must often suspend or revise a judgement as talk progresses, sometimes reinterpreting what transpired in the light of a finally revealed objective. A participant hears what is happening somewhat differently from an analyst or observer because his motive is different; he listens in order to respond appropriately, in order to decide what to do and say next.

Two Papers on Work in a Baby Clinic: (I) Standing Next to the Weighing Scales**

Dilys Daws

Dilys Daws

London

Dilys Daws  

I have been working for several years in the Baby Clinic of a General Practice in a Health Centre. One day weekly there are baby clinics, morning and afternoon, each taken by two of the G.P.s and the four Health Visitors attached to the Practice. A Nurse attends to give immunisations. I now go weekly to the morning clinics. I have contact with the other doctors in the practice and at times work closely with the practice's Social Worker who is a qualified psychotherapist.

I originally started to work at this Baby Clinic with a thesis that many mothers of new babies may have difficulties arising from their own personalities and from previous relationships, which become reflected in their dealings with the baby, or in disturbed behaviour of some kind in the baby. Mothers who had had no serious difficulties at other periods of their lives might have been thrown off balance by the experience of pregnancy, childbirth, and caring for a very new baby. I hoped that brief psychotherapeutic work of a combined interpretative and supportive nature could relieve some of these problems. Work could be directly with the mother, or mother and father, or by supporting the doctor or health visitor already involved with the family. The majority of babies are routinely brought for clinic visits by their mothers and I believe thisinfluences the nature of my referrals. I see more mothers and babies together than mothers and fathers and babies. Usually this seems an appropriate way of working; at other times it may be symptomatic of a marital or family problem**. In the several years I have worked in the Baby clinic I have felt my ambition to carry out short-term pieces of work has been justified.

The issues that have arisen over these years are of two main kinds. One is the nature of the clinical work undertaken. (Much of this presents as sleep problems and I give an account of this work in the companion paper which follows.) The second is the process of being a consultant to an institution other than one's own. I use the term “consultant” charily: it is not intended as a confusion with the medical use of the term.

Athol Hughes , Piera Furgiuele and Margherita Bianco

Margherita Bianco

Margherita Bianco  

Eating disorders have been discussed from the point of view of unconscious mechanisms since the first psychoanalytic investigations were made by Freud and Breuer in their work on hysteria. However, since then, the relationship of the symptom to the underlying unconscious dynamic has been investigated only sporadically. What Scott complained of in 1948, referred to in Tustin's paper of 1958, still pertains. That is that “as yet little has been done to trace the specific connections between the symptoms and the instinctive life, the imagination and the interpersonal relations”. Sohn (1973) stressed the envious attacks on the internal breast and the feeding mother. Wilson et al. (1983) reported several psychoanalytic studies which investigated the internal dynamics of anorexics and see the “fear of being fat” and the pathological body image of the anorexic as arising from an identification with a parent who has the same fear to a lesser extent. Thomä describes anorexia nervosa as a neurotic symptom complex; the symptom is an obsession, a “dominant idea” as an addiction that the patient tries to control by the intake or expulsion of food.

The overall impression in reading the literature is that there is no one cause, or determinant, underlying the symptom and that it occurs in a variety of character disorders that range from the borderline to the psychotic. One consistent feature is that it is ten to twenty times more frequent in adolescent females than in males, and that some investigators consider that non-eating in males is of a different order, with a different dynamic, than non-eating in females. Its greater frequency in females has led some investigators (for instance, Palazzol, 1978) to explain it from a family or from a psychosocial point of view. The fact that its incidence is on the increase, not only among middle class females, while it is practically unknown in the third world, indicates social factors at work in the selection of anorexia as a symptom, but that does not account for its dynamic. If one is starving, non-eating is not a way of controlling one's inner, or outer, objects. Nor can envy be considered to be ten to twenty times more operative in females than in males. Envy may be part of the picture but does not account for the high incidence of anorexia in females. Would it be possible to look at differences in the development of males and females that could lead the latter to express conflict in eating disorders, particularly at adolescence?

On Interpretation and Holding

Anne-Marie Sandler

Anne-Marie Sandler

35 Circus Road
London NW8 9JG

Anne-Marie Sandler  

When I was approached to give this paper as a contribution to a conference* entitled “Holding or Interpretation” I was not only honoured by the invitation but also excited by the challenge of the topic to be discussed. When I sat down to write the paper, however, I realised that most people, including myself, assume that they possess a relatively clear and simple idea of what is meant by “holding”. But when one does more than scratch the surface, it becomes clear that “holding” belongs to that class of concepts which are “elastic”, which change their meaning according to the context in which they are employed (J. Sandler, 1983). And certainly the concept as used in the literature covers a wide spectrum of meanings.

There is little doubt that the analytic situation, as developed by Freud, with its constant setting, its regular hours, its somewhat ritualised external trappings, provides the patient with a feeling of safety, a sense of being held. Winnicott (1965) was very aware of the relevance of the analytic setting to the patient, and gave special importance to it. For some particularly disturbed patients, he would arrange the cushions on the couch in a special way, so that they would find the cushions placed in the way they preferred. As we all know, Winnicott introduced the term “holding environment” as a metaphor for certain aspects of the analytic situation and the analytic process. The term derives from the maternal function of holding the infant, but taken as a metaphor, it has a much broader application, and extends beyond the infantile period — where the holding is literal and not metaphorical — to the broader caretaking function of the parent. Winnicott transferred this concept to an aspect of the analyst's function, with full awareness of the analyst's capacity to exercise a caretaking role. But for Winnicott this caretaking was always more than simple support and the provision of a reliable and reassuring presence. As Winnicott remarked, it “often takes the form of conveying in words, at the appropriate moment, something that shows that the analyst knows and understands the deepest anxiety that is being experienced, or that is waiting to be experienced”.

Sheila Spensley  

Introduction

The referral of this case for assessment for psychotherapy was, in part, an attempt to seek clarification of the diagnosis of one child's deeply disturbed and bizarre behaviour. It was also stimulated, and this has importance, by the interest, curiosity and bewilderment which the child herself was able to arouse in those caring for her.

Kate was eight years old and attending a school for the educationally subnormal when she was referred to the clinic by her school. Her teachers were convinced that Kate was of good intelligence and that she was wrongly placed in an E.S.N. school. There was a strongly held feeling that she had potential for development and her teachers were unhappy for her to remain in a setting where, it was believed, this potential would not be reached. Autism was suspected since Kate manifested many of the characteristics of the Kanner syndrome and the expectation was that she would benefit from more specialised schooling. So it was that Kate began to attend the clinic three times per week for the exploration of her strangeness and to consider whether she would qualify for special education. In addition, the function and fitness of psychotherapy in such an undertaking would also be kept in review.

What has resulted is that Kate has remained in psychotherapy for three years, and this has allowed close observation and study of her very primitive levels of experiencing and her consequent failures to achieve that degree of integration necessary for mentation. During this period, Kate's behaviour has been considered by both her parents and her teachers to be showing slow but steady improvements: in her responsiveness to and co-operation with others, in her use of language and in all the social and learning activities of school. This being so, it could at least be fairly said that psychotherapy was not contra-indicated. Any claim to there being a positive correlation between her “progress” and the therapy will have to wait on examination of the parallel changes in behaviour within the sessions in the course of the three years. It is this examination per se which is presented in this paper; a natural history, in this case, one of the products of psychotherapy.

A recent paper by Etchegoyan entitled Fifty Years After the Mutative Interpretation discusses at length James Strachey's famous 1934 essay, The Nature of the Therapeutic Action of Psychoanalysis (1983). Etchegoyan agrees with Strachey that for the neurotic vicious circle to be broken, the patient's distorted inner imaginative world of maternal and paternal objects has eventually to be differentiated from the real world. This “real” world is represented by what Strachey calls “the auxiliary superego” of the analyst. The function of auxiliary superego is exercised by means of the analyst's neutral attitude, which ensures that he neither plays in with the patient's “bad” superego which is being projected on to him, nor with his “good” one.

Etchegoyan says that for the gradual differentiation to take place, two conditions must apply — one necessary, the other sufficient. The necessary condition is the analytical setting, defined as the neutral attitude of the analyst. The sufficient condition is the interpretation. He points out that the neutral setting is necessary for the patient's personality and inner world of objects to unfold, but in order for the next stage to take place — that of differentiation of the unfolding inner world from the external one — the analyst has at his disposal a singular instrument, interpretation. I myself think that when Freud talked about analytic neutrality he meant it to apply also to the interpretive work.

I wish to return to Strachey's description of the two phases of a mutative interpretation later, but for the moment I would suggest that psychoanalytic work with children, especially with psychotic and borderline children, puts most fiercely to the test this notion of analytic neutrality. I do not wish to attack the notion of neutrality but I would like to undertake an examination of its meaning. Although I would hope what I say is relevant also to neurotic children, the excessive demands and needs of borderlines do serve to highlight the problem.

As the title of this paper indicates, the views expressed here are my own and not meant to be representative of any fixed “Kleinian” body of opinion. Indeed I should hope that every analyst, of whatever theoretical persuasion, would have his own individual way of observing and understanding the analytic process. Having said this there is no gainsaying the fact that there are differences of opinion about the validity of cerain ideas common to the colleagues and pupils of Melanie Klein; although clinical discussion, at least in the British Society, indicates that these differences are generally fewer than supposed, especially amongst child analysts. Broadly speaking I would imagine that all analysts subscribe to the fundamental theories of Freud; namely the theory of the life and death instincts, the Oedipus complex, the pleaure-pain principle, and the transference. The additional theories of Melanie Klein centre around the notions of the paranoid/schizoid and depressive positions, and the concept of projective identification. In more recent years I myself have drawn on the views of Bion, especially with respect to the relationship between the container and the contained, and the consequent clinical agoraphobic/claustrophobic phenomena. Following Bion I would also add the importance of dualism and the oscillation between opposites, for example, between omnipotence and helplessness, omniscience and ignorance, infantile and adult, neurosis and psychosis, etc.

Marta Smith and Maurice Whelan

Maurice Whelan

London

Maurice Whelan  

Introduction

This paper describes our work with a six year old child and his mother which consisted of ten sessions over a period of one year. The aim was to improve the mother/child relationship and to help the child's adjustment to life at home and in school by attempting to explore his internal world, fantasies and anxieties, using the child's play as a constant focal point.

It is our contention that far from being atypical, this case is increasingly representative of the work in community child guidance units. Perhaps it falls somewhere between extensive individual psychotherapy and well planned family therapy, and so we cannot rely on the theories of either to provide a theoretical framework. The extensive involvement by our clinic with the schools in our community allowed us to construct a new efficient team of school, family, therapist and social worker. The smooth functioning of the various parts of this network was a crucial factor in determining the outcome as no relevant aspect of the child's life was excluded from our minds.

Assessment phase

Ken was referred to us by his headteacher. His teacher had compiled an extensive report about his behaviour in class and included the observations of the school helpers and others involved with him. He was described as a child who did not smile but sought a lot of physical contact with adults. He was behaving aggressively towards other children, and on the few occasions he had seemed happy, he had become loud and bossy. Although, seemingly, a very bright child, he had no enthusiasm for school work. On very bad days he would cry for no obvious reason and if asked why he said he didn't know. He would calm down if comforted and then he would play a lot on his own, mainly with “Lego”. The teacher tried to help him understand his aggression to other children and their reluctance to play with him; he could agree that he was crying because he was feeling lonely. When the teacher wanted to see mother, she readily came to school and agreed that Ken was very difficult at home and welcomed the plan to refer to child guidance.

The concept of a borderline state or borderline personality is not new in psychiatry or psycho-analysis but it has become very fashionable in the last decade. Dr. Meltzer's aim is to remind us of the cardinal position that dream analysis occupies in the history, theory and practice of psychoanalysis, and to revive in us where necessary a fresh appetite for dreams. He has new ideas to offer. First, he runs through the theoretical background to these ideas by tracing once more his line of descent back through Bion and Klein to Freud. With Freud, who after all must be allowed a very special position in relation to the investigation of dreams since he thought of it first, Meltzer adopts an energetic and pugnacious approach. He is surprised to find such a difference and gap between the Freud whose work with the emotionality of patients could display such brilliance of intuition, such steadiness and clarity of response; and the Freud who found it more or less impossible to give emotionality a central place in his theories. Meltzer thinks that Freud's general theory of dreams is inadequate: although in practice Freud accorded dreams preeminence, in theory he underestimated their power and their function.

In this first section of his book Meltzer announces that he sees dreaming as linked with language development and artistic endeavour; he thus sees it as a process whose function is, as he says, to “generate meaning”. Dreaming is the mind perceived in its struggle to understand the truth of an emotional experience, the struggle to see and not to see things internal and external as they really are. To jump ahead with Meltzer's argument for a moment, he follows Bion in declaring that the mind needs truth as the body needs food: he sees dreaming as analagous to digestion, a process whereby a system works on what is fed into it to extract what is valuable and necessary for growth and maintenance.

This book is a new collection of Winnicott's writings, containing some papers and letters that have not hitherto been published, some that are uncollected and therefore not easily accessible, and some that are familiar and readily available, all on the related themes of deprivation and delinquency. They cover a long time-span, between 1939, (when Winnicott first became interested and involved in the problem of wartime evacuation of small children, hence the link between deprivation and the antisocial tendency) to 1970, only months before his death (when addressing the Association of Workers for Maladjusted Children on “Residential Care as Therapy”).

The book is divided into three main sections, with a short fourth dealing with psychotherapeutic interactions with antisocial children. The first part deals with what Winnicott made of his wartime experiences, many of the papers being in fact broadcasts to ordinary parents and foster parents of evacuated children. This section is outstanding for his facility in conveying complex and sometimes painful emotional realities to non-professionals in a way that is never patronising and yet feels as if it must have brought considerable advances in understanding to those caught up in the domestic upheavals of the time. He brings Bowlby's work on early separation into the context of what was then everyday experience, and puts it to very good use in his own words on evacuation and the return therefrom. The respect and value that he accords ordinary, good-enough parenting and his emphasis on the importance of the child's own home, however rich or poor, must have made his message accessible and comforting to many a troubled mother and father. One cannot help admiring the complete absence of professional arrogance, unnecessary jargon or judgemental attitudes. He achieves a blend of psychoanalytical understanding, tough common sense and great humanity that impresses one throughout the volume.

The second part of the book explains Winnicott's theoretical position on deprivation, the antisocial tendency and delinquency, while the third addresses some of the provisions society can make for children suffering in this way. Since all the sections are each in roughly chronological order, in reading through the book the overall development of Winnicott's thinking on these themes is not clearly delineated; in fact, especially in the theoretical section, the order of the papers is at times perplexing and one can forget the chronology quite easily.

Isabel Lyth  

Introduction

The theoretical basis for the thinking in this paper centres on a particular aspect of the development of the self, development that takes place through introjective identification. Healthy development depends greatly on the availability of appropriate models of individuals, relationships and situations for such identification. These models may be found in the adults who care for the children, their relationship with the children and with each other, and the setting for care. Healthy development may also require the management of the child's identification with inappropriate models, for example with other children in institutions for delinquent or maladjusted children.

Institutionalised children are likely to find their most significant models for identification within the institution itself, both in the institution as a whole and its sub-systems and in individual staff members and children. This leads to the concept of the institution as a therapeutic milieu whose primary task may be defined as providing conditions for healthy development and/or providing therapy for damaged children. Thus all the child's experiences in the institution contribute positively or negatively to his development, not only those more narrowly defined as education, individual or group therapy or child care. Indeed it has been the author's experience that the benefits of such provisions may well be counteracted by more general features of the institution.

This formulation would then lead one to take a very wide view of the institution in considering its effectiveness in carrying out its primary task. One would include its whole way of functioning; its management structure, including its division into sub-systems and how those relate to each other; the nature of authority and how that is operated; the social defence system built into the institution; its culture and traditions. In line with the theme of this paper, one would consider these in the context of how far they facilitate the provision of healthy models for identification, or alternatively inhibit the provision of such models.
